say.text: A 38-year-old woman has a painless, solitary thyroid nodule. She is euthyroid, and the lump has been there six months.
Your exam paper asks for the **first investigation**. What do you order?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what you must know about the nodule's function, and whether its look is suspicious, before you spend a needle on it.
That choice is not right. It tempts because older exam papers keyed FNAC as the first test, and FNAC is the test that judges what a nodule is.
But 'first' and 'best for the nature of the nodule' are different questions. Ask what must be known before a needle goes in.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the verb in the stem: the exam key and current practice differ on this exact word, 'first'.

say.text: That choice is not right. A radionuclide scan tempts because it sorts a nodule into hot or cold, which sounds like a good first split.
But a scan is not done for every nodule. It is used only when a result already in hand calls for it. Which result would you need first?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what triggers a scan before you use one.

say.text: Yes. Serum TSH and neck ultrasound come first. TSH tells you whether a scan is needed, and ultrasound shows features that make a nodule suspicious.
Some older papers still key FNAC as the first step, so you need the reason too.
Two questions hide in the word 'first'. The first investigation is TSH and ultrasound. FNAC is the investigation of choice for the nature of the nodule.
PYQs expected FNAC as 'first', but current practice starts with TSH and ultrasound. Learn both, and read the verb in each stem.
The same nodule, but this time her TSH comes back low.
What do you do next?

choices.label: Radionuclide scan for a hot nodule
Ultrasound-guided FNAC of the nodule now
FNAC and scan together, straight away
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: A low TSH points to the nodule's function. Which test looks at function, and does it need a needle?
That choice is not right. FNAC tempts because it is the test for the nature of a nodule, so it feels like the next step whatever the TSH shows.
But a low TSH points to function. A hot nodule is rarely malignant and usually needs no FNAC, so sampling it now is the wrong step.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so notice that the old key is talking. A low TSH changes the question.

say.text: That choice is not right. Doing both at once feels thorough, and it matches the habit of sampling every nodule.
But most nodules are benign, so the function result decides whether a needle is needed at all. Which result comes first?

sure_note.text: You were sure, but a needle is chosen by the result, not by habit.

say.text: Yes. A low TSH sends you to a radionuclide scan, which looks for a hot, hyperfunctioning nodule.
A hot nodule is rarely malignant, so FNAC is not the first step for it.
A cold nodule, one that does not take up iodine, carries a higher risk than a hot one, but most cold nodules are still benign.
So the scan sorts hot from cold. A cold nodule that looks suspicious on ultrasound is the one that needs FNAC.
Ultrasound is the second filter. Suspicious features include hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, a taller-than-wide shape and irregular margins.
Only about 5 to 15 percent of nodules are malignant, which is why the filters keep most patients away from needles.
FNAC is reported as Bethesda IV, a follicular neoplasm. The surgeon asks whether this is carcinoma.
Which test settles it?

choices.label: Frozen section of the nodule during surgery
Histology of the resected lobe for invasion
Repeat FNAC with a finer ultrasound needle
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the feature that defines a follicular carcinoma, and about which specimen can show it.
That choice is not right. It tempts because FNAC judges the nature of the nodule, so a better needle feels like a better answer.
But cytology alone cannot make the diagnosis here. Which tissue would show the capsule?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again at 'carcinoma'. A finer needle still gives a cell sample.

say.text: That choice is not right. A frozen section sounds like a quick histology answer, which is why it tempts you.
But frozen section is of little value here, so a quick slide cannot settle it. Which tissue, examined in full, shows the capsule?

sure_note.text: You were sure. Frozen section is histology, but it does not settle a follicular lesion.

say.text: Yes. Follicular carcinoma is diagnosed only by capsular or vascular invasion on histology.
FNAC can report the lesion as Bethesda IV but cannot separate adenoma from carcinoma.
Invasion is a feature of tissue, and FNAC samples cells. So FNAC can only report a follicular neoplasm, Bethesda IV.
Frozen section is of little value for the same reason, so the resected lobe on histology decides.
Which finding separates follicular carcinoma from follicular adenoma?

choices.label: Capsular or vascular invasion on histology
A Bethesda IV report on FNAC
Follicular pattern on the cytology smear
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which of these a needle can see, and which one only a whole specimen can show.
That choice is not right. A Bethesda IV report tempts because it is the label on every follicular lesion you will see.
But a label says the lesion is a follicular neoplasm. It does not say whether invasion is present. What does?

sure_note.text: You were sure. A report label is not a diagnosis, so check what it leaves out.

say.text: That choice is not right. A follicular pattern looks like the diagnosis on a smear, which is why it tempts you.
But adenoma can show the same cell pattern. What can a needle never see?

sure_note.text: You were sure. Cell pattern is shared by adenoma and carcinoma, so pattern alone cannot separate them.

say.text: Yes. Invasion across the capsule or into vessels is a histology feature, so only the resected lobe can show it.
A needle samples cells, and cells cannot show invasion. So FNAC names the lesion as a follicular neoplasm, and it cannot name carcinoma.
Frozen section is of little value either, so the resected lobe on histology decides.
